lessons.title: The sales mindset (for people who hate "selling")

steps.body: Everything before this was preparation. Sales is where English becomes income. And here's the reframe: selling isn't convincing people to buy things they don't need. It's **helping a client see that their problem is solvable, by you, at a fair price.** The freelancers who starve aren't the unskilled ones — they're the ones who can't say their price out loud without apologizing.

Three beliefs to install:

1. **You're not begging; you're offering.** Begging: *"Please give me a chance sir."* Offering: *"I can solve this problem. Here's the price. Interested?"* Same person, different posture. Clients buy from the second one.
2. **Price is information, not a confession.** Say your price the way you'd say the time: flat, calm, no apology. *"The Standard package is $150."* Full stop. The moment you add *"but we can negotiate..."* unprompted, you've told them the price was fake.
3. **"No" is data, not rejection.** Every "too expensive" teaches you about your positioning. The response is never panic — it's Lesson 7.3.

steps.title: Negotiation lines (audio)
steps.tip: Say them until they feel like your own words.

steps.prompt:
**Spot the desperation**

Find the 6 sales mistakes in this message (then rewrite it):
"Dear Sir, I am very interested in your project sir. I am highly skilled and can do any work at cheap rates. My price is $50 but I can do $30 for you sir, just give me one chance please. I guarantee 100% satisfaction. Waiting for your kind reply."
Mistakes: (1) "Dear Sir" + "sir" ×3 — begging tone; (2) "highly skilled" — unverifiable; (3) "any work" — no one believes it; (4) "cheap rates" + instant self-discount $50→$30 — prices are fiction; (5) "100% guarantee" — client-safety violation; (6) no specific offer, no proof, no next step.

lessons.title: Scope → price: the chain that protects you

steps.body:
Amateurs discuss; professionals scope. The chain, in order — never skip a link:

1. **Scope in one paragraph:** what IS included, what is NOT. No "etc.", no "full solution", no "complete package". Concrete nouns only.
2. **Tiered pricing (3 tiers, fixed prices):** Basic / Standard / Premium. The middle tier is the one you want them to pick — make it the obvious value. Never hourly as a beginner (clients fear open-ended meters).
3. **Say it once, then silence.** After stating the price, stop talking. The silence feels eternal; it's usually 5 seconds. Whoever speaks first loses positioning.

**Model scope + tiers** (adapt to your real offer):
steps.example:
Scope: clean 12 months of sales Excel data; build one Streamlit dashboard (sales by product, city, month + top customers); deploy to a browser link. Not included: POS connection, mobile app, data entry. One revision round included.
Basic — $80: dashboard from your Excel file, 1 revision round. Standard — $150 (most popular): everything in Basic + monthly auto-update setup + 2 revision rounds. Premium — $250: everything in Standard + 30-min training call + 30 days support.

steps.title: The price conversation, aloud
steps.text:
Read both parts aloud, twice — once as the client (feel their hesitation), once as you (practice the calm):
Client: "So... what's the damage?"
You: "For the Standard package — dashboard, auto-updates, two revision rounds, 30 days of support — it's $150 fixed. 50% to start, 50% on delivery."
(silence — count to 5 in your head, don't fill it)
Client: "Hmm, that's more than I expected."
You: "I hear you. What were you hoping to stay around?"
Client: "Maybe $80?"
You: "Got it. At $80 I can do the Basic — dashboard from your Excel file, one revision round. The auto-update setup and the extra revision round are what make the Standard $150. Which fits better — or want me to walk through the difference once more?"
Note the moves: price stated flat, silence held, budget asked (not assumed), smaller
steps.tip: Shadow 0.5–1 sec behind the speaker. Copy the music, not just the words.

steps.body: This is the moment most beginners lose. The script:

1. **Agree, don't defend:** *"Totally understand — budgets matter."* (Never argue with their budget. It's real to them.)
2. **Restate the value:** *"At $150 you get [X, Y, Z + support]."* (Remind them what the number buys. Briefly.)
3. **Offer a smaller scope — never a smaller price for the same work:** *"If $60 is the budget, I can do a smaller version: [reduced scope] for $70."* (Discounting the same work teaches them your prices are fiction.)
4. **Name the risk of cheap, not the competitor:** *"What I'd avoid is promising the full thing for $60 — that's how projects end up half-done."* (Never badmouth the $60 guy. Make cheap sound risky, not him sound bad.)
5. **Hand back the choice:** *"Want the smaller scope, or should I walk you through what the full one includes?"*

steps.heading: If they still say no
steps.body: *"No problem at all — if things change, I'm here. Want me to send over the smaller-scope details anyway, in case it's useful later?"* Leave the door open. A graceful no often becomes a yes in 3 months.

steps.title: Say your price on a call
steps.prompt: 60 seconds of planning (3 bullets: scope recap, price, payment terms). Then 60 seconds of speaking: deliver your price for Sana's project as if she's on the call. Record it. Listen: did you apologize? Rush? Add "but we can negotiate"? Redo until the price lands flat and calm.
steps.tip: Fluency mode: no stopping, no mid-sentence correcting.

lessons.title: Selling your time (boundaries are the product)

steps.body:
Your time is inventory. Every "yes" to free work is stock given away:

- **Free samples:** never. Paid pilot instead (Module 5, scenario 6).
- **"One small change" #5:** priced (Module 5, scenario 9).
- **Cousin/friend discounts:** same quality, same price — or a smaller scope. A "family rate" teaches your whole network that your work is cheap.
- **Urgency pricing:** *"I can rush this — delivery in 3 days instead of 7 — with a 25% rush fee. Or standard timeline at the quoted price."* Urgency is a premium feature, not a favor.

steps.heading: The sentence that saves freelancers
steps.body: *"Happy to do it — since that's outside our agreed scope, it's $X extra. Want me to add it?"* Friendly. Firm. Final.
Ten things clients actually say, and the one-line move for each. Memorize the *moves*, not the scripts.

Client says · Your move
"Too expensive." · Agree → restate value → offer smaller scope (never a discount on the same work)
"Another guy is cheaper." · "What I'd avoid is promising the full thing for $60 — that's how projects end up half-done."
"Can you do it faster?" · "I can rush it — 25% rush fee for 3-day delivery, or standard timeline at the quoted price."
"Just do a free sample first." · "I don't do free samples — but I offer a $30 paid pilot, deducted from the full quote if you continue."
"I'll think about it." · "Of course. Is it the price, the timeline, or something else you're unsure about?" (diagnose, don't wait)
"Can you also add [big thing]?" · "Happy to — that's outside our scope, so it's $X extra. Or phase 2 next week. Which works better?"
"My cousin wants it cheaper." · "Same quality, same price — or I can scope a smaller version for him. I don't do family discounts on the same work."
"Guarantee the results?" · "I guarantee the work — [concrete deliverables]. What I can't guarantee is [outcome], because that depends on [their data/market]. Anyone who guarantees that is guessing."
"Why should I trust you?" · "Fair question. Here's a demo of real work: [link]. And we start with a small paid pilot — low risk for both of us."
Goes silent for a week · One nudge (day 3) → clean pause (day 10) → stop chasing. Chasing destroys positioning.

steps.rule: 8/10 to move on. Answer first, then learn from the misses.

steps.heading: Can-do statements
steps.body:
- [ ] I can state my price flatly, without apology or unprompted discounting
- [ ] I can run the full "too expensive" script: agree → value → smaller scope → risk of cheap → choice
- [ ] I can write scope + 3-tier pricing for any small data project
- [ ] I hold the silence after stating a price
- [ ] I never do free work, never badmouth competitors, never guarantee results

steps.heading: Mini-test (the final exam)
steps.body: Run a full 15-minute mock sales call with your AI tutor as a budget-conscious client: discovery → scope → price → handle "too expensive" → close with a next step. Record it. This is the single artifact that proves the course worked. Compare it against your Module 0 placement recording — play 60 seconds of each back-to-back. You'll hear the 90 days.

steps.heading: Re-entry note
steps.body:
Sales is a practiced reflex. One mock price conversation per week (Drill 7.3) keeps it sharp forever.

💰 **Badge earned: Closer** — all 8 badges collected. You are client-ready.
